what_it_does: Smart labels, wearable health patches, and textile-embedded sensors need processors that cost a few cents, bend like paper, and draw almost no power — requirements that ordinary silicon chips cannot meet. This paper proposes a methodology for automatically building ultra-minimal RISC-V processors (RISC-V is an open, freely usable processor instruction standard) that implement only the instructions a specific application actually uses, then physically printing them on flexible plastic film instead of rigid silicon.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A conventional processor supports hundreds of instructions so it can run any program. But a specific application — say, detecting atrial fibrillation from a wearable ECG sensor — only ever uses a small subset of those instructions (the paper finds 24–86% of the instruction set goes unused across a range of real applications). Every unused instruction still takes up chip area and leaks power. The RISSP (RISC-V Instruction Subset Processor) methodology strips those away.

How it works. The process has three steps.

1. Profile the application. Compile the application's C code using the standard RISC-V compiler targeting the compact RV32E instruction set (a reduced 32-bit variant with 16 registers). Inspect which distinct instructions appear in the compiled output — typically 10 to 30 out of about 40 possible.

2. Assemble from pre-verified blocks. Every RISC-V instruction has been pre-coded and formally verified as a standalone hardware description — a self-contained digital building block analogous to a Lego brick. Pull only the needed blocks from this library, connect them with a simple case-select switch (ModularEX), and attach standard memory and register-file interfaces. The synthesis tool (electronic design automation software that converts the description to an actual circuit layout) automatically finds and merges shared logic across blocks, so no expert tuning is needed.

3. Fabricate on flexible film. The resulting circuit blueprint is handed to Pragmatic Semiconductor's 0.6-micrometer IGZO FlexIC process — a technology that prints transistors made from a metal-oxide semiconductor onto a thin plastic (polyimide) wafer rather than silicon, making the chip 30 micrometers thick, physically bendable, and manufacturable at very low cost.

The key design choice. Treating each instruction as a pre-verified, self-contained module — rather than modifying a monolithic processor — means correctness carries over automatically and no re-verification is needed when assembling a new subset.

The catch. For long-lived devices that need software updates, an AI tool rewrites any newly compiled instructions that fall outside the supported subset using equivalent sequences from within the subset, at a code-size overhead of 5–36%.

The result. RISSPs use 8–43% less chip area and 3–30% less power than a full RISC-V processor on the same flexible process, and are about 40 times more energy-efficient per instruction than Serv, the previously smallest known 32-bit RISC-V processor.
